All the code in this series is available on GitHub. Clone it, run it, and try breaking it yourself.

georgekobaidze / dotnet11-playground

A lightweight playground repository for experimenting with and testing new features introduced in .NET 11 and C# 15.

.NET 11 & C# 15 Playground

A lightweight playground repository for experimenting with and testing new features introduced in .NET 11 and C# 15.

Use it to explore language changes, try out APIs, and validate ideas in isolation without production constraints. Each feature lives in its own small project, often with a "before" and "after" version so you can see what the new feature actually changes.

What's inside

Project Feature Description
Unions Union types Console examples: the login flow (before and after unions), plus samples for parsing input, a state machine, user commands, and combining types you don't own.
UnionsWebApi Union types A minimal API that returns a union from a service and maps each outcome to an HTTP response.

More examples will be added as new features are explored.

Getting started

You'll need the .NET 11 SDK. Then clone the repo and run any example:

dotnet run
…
View on GitHub

Follow me on GitHub for more updates!

Table of Contents

  • One Last Round with Unions
  • 1. Parsing and Validating Input
  • 2. Returning Results from an API
  • 3. Modeling a State Machine
  • 4. Handling Commands from User Input
  • 5. Combining Types You Don't Own
  • When Not to Use Unions
  • Wrapping Up

One Last Round with Unions

The last two articles in this series were all about unions. In the first one, we looked at what unions are and whether we actually need them. In the second one, we popped the hood and found a struct.

.NET 11 has a lot more to offer, so I promise this is the last union article in the series.

And this time, it's all about practice. We're software engineers. We don't really trust a new feature until we've used it to solve a real problem. That's where its value shows up.

So no theory and no IL this time. Just five common problems, the workarounds we've all written for them, and how unions solve each one better:

  1. Parsing and validating input
  2. Returning results from an API
  3. Modeling a state machine
  4. Handling commands from user input
  5. Combining types you don't own

Every example is runnable, and all the code is in the GitHub repository.

The four console examples live in src/Unions (uncomment the one you want in Program.cs), and the API example is a separate project in src/UnionsWebApi:

dotnet run --project src/Unions
dotnet run --project src/UnionsWebApi

1. Parsing and Validating Input

Every app takes input it can't trust: console input, query strings, config files, CSV rows. Parsing can go wrong in more than one way, and the caller usually needs to know which way.

Let's parse a user's age. It has to be a number, and it has to be realistic.

The Old Way

The classic TryParse pattern tells you that something failed, but not why:

static bool TryParseAge(string input, out int age)
{
    if (!int.TryParse(input, out age))
        return false;

    return age is >= 0 and <= 150;
}

Was it "abc"? Was it "-5"? The caller gets false and has to guess, so the user sees a vague "Invalid age."

The other classic approach is to throw:

static int ParseAge(string input)
{
    if (!int.TryParse(input, out int age))
        throw new FormatException($"'{input}' is not a number.");

    if (age is < 0 or > 150)
        throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(input), $"{age} is not a realistic age.");

    return age;
}

Now we have the reason, but we're using exceptions for something that happens all the time. Users mistype things constantly. Nothing in the signature warns the caller to catch them, either. int ParseAge(string) looks like it always succeeds.

The Union Way 

public record ParseError(string Message);

public union ParseResult<T>(T, ParseError);

public static class AgeParser
{
    public static ParseResult<int> Parse(string input)
    {
        if (!int.TryParse(input, out int age))
            return new ParseError($"'{input}' is not a number.");

        if (age is < 0 or > 150)
            return new ParseError($"{age} is not a realistic age.");

        return age;
    }
}

And a small console loop to try it out:

while (true)
{
    Console.Write("Enter your age: ");
    string? input = Console.ReadLine();

    if (input is null)
        break; // the input stream was closed (Ctrl+Z on Windows, Ctrl+D on macOS/Linux)

    string message = AgeParser.Parse(input) switch
    {
        int age => $"Got it, you're {age}.",
        ParseError error => $"Oops: {error.Message}"
    };

    Console.WriteLine(message);
}

Type 34, then abc, then 200, and you get a clear answer for each.

Why It's Better

  • The reason travels with the result. Instead of a bare false, the caller gets a ParseError with a message it can show the user.
  • The signature tells the truth. ParseResult<int> says "you'll get an int or an error" right in the method signature. Nobody has to read the implementation to find out what can go wrong.
  • You can't forget the failure case. To get the int out, you have to match on the union, and the compiler makes sure the ParseError arm is there.
  • No exceptions for normal input. Bad input is expected, not exceptional. Exceptions stay reserved for real bugs.
  • It's reusable. ParseResult<T> is generic, so the same union works for ParseResult<DateOnly>, ParseResult<Uri>, or anything else you parse.

2. Returning Results from an API

Most API endpoints have more than one outcome. Looking up a user, for example: the user exists, the user doesn't exist, or the user exists but you're not allowed to see them.

The Old Way

Usually, each outcome gets a different mechanism. "Not found" becomes null. "Forbidden" becomes an exception:

public User? GetUser(int id)
{
    if (!_users.TryGetValue(id, out User? user))
        return null;

    if (user.Id == AdminId)
        throw new UnauthorizedAccessException("Admin profiles are private.");

    return user;
}

And the endpoint has to deal with both:

app.MapGet("/users/{id}", (int id, UserService users) =>
{
    try
    {
        User? user = users.GetUser(id);
        return user is null ? Results.NotFound() : Results.Ok(user);
    }
    catch (UnauthorizedAccessException ex)
    {
        return Results.Problem(ex.Message, statusCode: StatusCodes.Status403Forbidden);
    }
});

The signature User? GetUser(int id) only tells half the story. You can guess that null means "not found", but nothing tells you about the exception. Forget the try/catch, and a perfectly normal "you can't see this" turns into a 500 error.

The Union Way 

public record User(int Id, string Name);
public record UserNotFound(int Id);
public record AccessDenied(string Reason);

public union GetUserResult(User, UserNotFound, AccessDenied);

public class UserService
{
    private const int AdminId = 100;

    private readonly Dictionary<int, User> _users = new()
    {
        [1] = new User(1, "Ada"),
        [2] = new User(2, "Linus"),
        [AdminId] = new User(AdminId, "Admin"),
    };

    public GetUserResult GetUser(int id)
    {
        if (!_users.TryGetValue(id, out User? user))
            return new UserNotFound(id);

        if (user.Id == AdminId)
            return new AccessDenied("Admin profiles are private.");

        return user;
    }
}

And the endpoint maps each outcome to an HTTP response in one place:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
builder.Services.AddSingleton<UserService>();

var app = builder.Build();

app.MapGet("/users/{id}", (int id, UserService users) =>
    users.GetUser(id) switch
    {
        User user => Results.Ok(user),
        UserNotFound notFound => Results.NotFound($"User {notFound.Id} doesn't exist."),
        AccessDenied denied => Results.Problem(denied.Reason, statusCode: StatusCodes.Status403Forbidden)
    });

app.Run();

Run it and try all three outcomes:

curl -i http://localhost:5115/users/1    # 200 OK
curl -i http://localhost:5115/users/99   # 404 Not Found
curl -i http://localhost:5115/users/100  # 403 Forbidden

Note: Port 5115 is what the app uses on my machine. Your port may be different, especially if you created your own project. Use the URL printed in the console when the app starts.

Why It's Better

  • Every outcome is in the signature. GetUserResult tells you there are exactly three possibilities, and what each one carries.
  • One mechanism instead of two. No mix of null and exceptions. Every outcome is just a value.
  • The service doesn't know about HTTP. UserService returns domain results, not IResult or status codes. The endpoint decides how each one becomes a response, so the same service works for a gRPC call, a background job, or a test.
  • New outcomes can't slip through. Add a UserSuspended case later, and the compiler flags the endpoint until you decide what HTTP status it gets.

Why not Results.Forbid()? It looks like the obvious choice for a 403, but it hands the request to the authentication system. If your app has no authentication configured, it throws at runtime. Results.Problem(..., statusCode: 403) works everywhere.

3. Modeling a State Machine

Lots of things in software move through states: a network connection, an order, a payment, a background job. Each state usually comes with its own data. A connection that's connecting knows which attempt it's on. A connected one knows when it connected. A failed one knows why.

The Old Way

The usual approach is an enum for the state, plus a property for every piece of data any state might need:

public enum ConnectionStatus { Disconnected, Connecting, Connected, Failed }

public class Connection
{
    public ConnectionStatus Status { get; set; }
    public int? Attempt { get; set; }                    // only when Connecting
    public DateTimeOffset? ConnectedSince { get; set; }  // only when Connected
    public string? FailureReason { get; set; }           // only when Failed
}

Those comments are doing a lot of work. Nothing stops Status from being Connected while ConnectedSince is null and FailureReason is set. Every reader has to remember which fields are valid in which state, and every property is nullable, so the code fills up with ? and !.

Even the switch can't be fully trusted:

string Describe(Connection c) => c.Status switch
{
    ConnectionStatus.Disconnected => "Offline",
    ConnectionStatus.Connecting => $"Connecting (attempt {c.Attempt})...",
    ConnectionStatus.Connected => $"Online since {c.ConnectedSince:T}",
    ConnectionStatus.Failed => $"Failed: {c.FailureReason}",
    _ => "Unknown"
};

An enum is just a number underneath, so (ConnectionStatus)42 is a valid value. The compiler warns unless you add a _ arm, and that arm swallows any new state you add later.

The Union Way

Each state becomes a record that carries only its own data:

public record Disconnected;
public record Connecting(int Attempt);
public record Connected(DateTimeOffset Since);
public record Failed(string Reason);

public union ConnectionState(Disconnected, Connecting, Connected, Failed);

The transitions live in one place:

public static class ConnectionMachine
{
    private const int MaxAttempts = 3;

    public static ConnectionState Next(ConnectionState state, bool serverResponds) => state switch
    {
        Disconnected => new Connecting(1),
        Connecting when serverResponds => new Connected(DateTimeOffset.Now),
        Connecting c when c.Attempt < MaxAttempts => new Connecting(c.Attempt + 1),
        Connecting => new Failed($"No response after {MaxAttempts} attempts."),
        Connected when serverResponds => state,
        Connected => new Disconnected(),
        Failed => new Disconnected()
    };

    public static string Describe(ConnectionState state) => state switch
    {
        Disconnected => "Offline",
        Connecting c => $"Connecting (attempt {c.Attempt})...",
        Connected c => $"Online since {c.Since:T}",
        Failed f => $"Failed: {f.Reason}"
    };
}

And a small loop lets you play the server:

ConnectionState state = new Disconnected();

while (true)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"State: {ConnectionMachine.Describe(state)}");
    Console.Write("Does the server respond? (y/n): ");
    string? input = Console.ReadLine();

    if (input is null)
        break; // the input stream was closed (Ctrl+Z on Windows, Ctrl+D on macOS/Linux)

    state = ConnectionMachine.Next(state, serverResponds: input.Trim().ToLower() == "y");
    Console.WriteLine();
}

Answer n three times while connecting and watch it fail. Answer y and it connects. Answer n while connected and it drops back to offline.

Why It's Better

  • Impossible states can't exist. There's no way to build a Connected without a Since date, or a Failed without a reason. The data and the state are the same thing.
  • No nullable fields. Connected.Since is a plain DateTimeOffset. You never check for null because the value can't be missing.
  • All transitions in one exhaustive switch. Reading Next tells you the whole state machine at a glance.
  • New states can't be forgotten. Add a Reconnecting state, and the compiler flags both Next and Describe until you handle it. No _ arm to hide it.

4. Handling Commands from User Input

Command-line tools, chat bots and game consoles all do the same thing: read a line of text, figure out which command it is, and run it. The parsing and the running tend to get tangled together.

Let's build a tiny to-do list with four commands: add, done, list and quit.

The Old Way

The usual approach is one big switch on strings, with parsing, validation and execution all mixed together:

switch (parts[0])
{
    case "add":
        if (parts.Length < 2)
        {
            Console.WriteLine("What should I add?");
            break;
        }
        items.Add(parts[1]);
        break;

    case "done":
        if (parts.Length < 2 || !int.TryParse(parts[1], out int number))
        {
            Console.WriteLine("Which item?");
            break;
        }
        items.RemoveAt(number - 1);
        break;

    case "list":
        // print the items...
        break;

    case "quit":
        return;

    default:
        Console.WriteLine("Unknown command.");
        break;
}

It works for four commands. At fifteen, it's a wall of code. The command logic can't be tested without the console, "add" is just a string that's easy to mistype, and adding a new command means digging through the whole block.

The Union Way

First, each command becomes a record that carries exactly the data it needs:

public record Add(string Text);
public record Done(int Number);
public record ShowList;
public record Quit;
public record Invalid(string Reason);

public union Command(Add, Done, ShowList, Quit, Invalid);

Then parsing happens in one place, and only there:

public static class CommandParser
{
    public static Command Parse(string input)
    {
        string[] parts = input.Trim().Split(' ', 2, StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries);

        if (parts.Length == 0)
            return new Invalid("Type a command: add, done, list or quit.");

        string argument = parts.Length > 1 ? parts[1] : "";

        return parts[0].ToLowerInvariant() switch
        {
            "add" when argument.Length > 0 => new Add(argument),
            "add" => new Invalid("What should I add? Try: add Buy milk"),
            "done" when int.TryParse(argument, out int number) => new Done(number),
            "done" => new Invalid("Which item? Try: done 1"),
            "list" => new ShowList(),
            "quit" => new Quit(),
            _ => new Invalid($"Unknown command '{parts[0]}'.")
        };
    }
}

And running a command never deals with strings again:

public class TodoList
{
    private readonly List<string> _items = [];

    public string Execute(Command command) => command switch
    {
        Add add => AddItem(add.Text),
        Done done => Complete(done.Number),
        ShowList => Show(),
        Quit => "Bye!",
        Invalid invalid => invalid.Reason
    };

    private string AddItem(string text)
    {
        _items.Add(text);
        return $"Added: {text}";
    }

    private string Complete(int number)
    {
        if (number < 1 || number > _items.Count)
            return $"There's no item {number}.";

        string item = _items[number - 1];
        _items.RemoveAt(number - 1);
        return $"Done: {item}";
    }

    private string Show() =>
        _items.Count == 0
            ? "Nothing to do. Nice!"
            : string.Join(Environment.NewLine, _items.Select((item, i) => $"{i + 1}. {item}"));
}

Finally, the loop that ties it together:

var todo = new TodoList();
Console.WriteLine("Commands: add <text>, done <number>, list, quit");

while (true)
{
    Console.Write("> ");
    string? line = Console.ReadLine();

    if (line is null)
        break; // the input stream was closed (Ctrl+Z on Windows, Ctrl+D on macOS/Linux)

    Command command = CommandParser.Parse(line);
    Console.WriteLine(todo.Execute(command));

    if (command is Quit)
        break;
}

Try add Buy milk, add Write the next article, list, done 1, and list again.

Why It's Better

  • Parse once, then work with types. Text only exists at the edge, in CommandParser. Everything after that works with real types. Done carries an int, not a string that might be a number.
  • Each piece has one job. The parser turns text into commands, and TodoList runs them. You can test the parser without a to-do list, and the to-do list without a console.
  • The _ arm stays where it belongs. Strings can be anything, so the parser needs a fallback. But Execute matches on the union, so it needs no _ arm and stays fully checked.
  • New commands can't be half-added. Add a Rename record to the union, and the compiler flags Execute until you handle it. You can't forget the second half of the work.

5. Combining Types You Don't Own

Sometimes a value can be one of several types you didn't write and can't change. Think of IDs coming from different systems: an old database uses int, the CRM uses string codes, and the new cloud service uses Guid.

The Old Way

Option one is to give up on types and use object:

static string ToKey(object id) => id switch
{
    int number => $"legacy-{number}",
    string code => $"crm-{code}",
    Guid guid => $"cloud-{guid:N}",
    _ => throw new ArgumentException($"Unsupported ID type: {id.GetType().Name}")
};

The signature accepts anything. ToKey(3.14) and ToKey(DateTime.Now) both compile, and you only find out at runtime.

Option two is to wrap every type in your own hierarchy:

public abstract record ExternalId;
public sealed record LegacyId(int Value) : ExternalId;
public sealed record CrmId(string Value) : ExternalId;
public sealed record CloudId(Guid Value) : ExternalId;

That's type-safe, but now you need three wrapper classes for values that were perfectly fine on their own, and every caller has to write new LegacyId(1042) instead of just 1042.

The Union Way 

public union ExternalId(int, string, Guid);

That's it. No wrappers, no base class. int, string and Guid are case types as they are:

public static class IdMapper
{
    public static ExternalId Parse(string input)
    {
        input = input.Trim();

        if (int.TryParse(input, out int number))
            return number;

        if (Guid.TryParse(input, out Guid guid))
            return guid;

        return input;
    }

    public static string ToKey(ExternalId id) => id switch
    {
        int number => $"legacy-{number}",
        string code => $"crm-{code}",
        Guid guid => $"cloud-{guid:N}"
    };
}

A small loop to try it:

while (true)
{
    Console.Write("Enter an ID: ");
    string? input = Console.ReadLine();

    if (input is null)
        break; // the input stream was closed (Ctrl+Z on Windows, Ctrl+D on macOS/Linux)

    ExternalId id = IdMapper.Parse(input);
    Console.WriteLine($"Key: {IdMapper.ToKey(id)}");
}

Try 1042, ACME-77, and a GUID like 3f2504e0-4f89-11d3-9a0c-0305e82c3301.

Compare that to the object version. There, ToKey(3.14) compiles fine and only crashes at runtime, when the _ => throw arm fires. With the union, the same mistake doesn't even compile:

IdMapper.ToKey(1042);       // ✅ an int: compiles
IdMapper.ToKey("ACME-77");  // ✅ a string: compiles
IdMapper.ToKey(3.14);       // ❌ a double: compile error, double isn't one of the case types

Why It's Better

  • No wrapper classes. Types you don't own can be case types directly. No class hierarchy can do that, because you can't make int inherit from your base class.
  • Type-safe, unlike object. The signature says "an int, a string or a Guid", and the compiler enforces it at every call site.
  • Exhaustive, unlike object. No _ => throw arm. Add a long case later, and the compiler shows you every switch to update.

One Thing to Keep in Mind: Boxing

As we saw in the previous article, a union stores its value in an object? Value property. int and Guid are value types, so every time an ExternalId holds one, the value gets boxed: copied into a small object on the heap.

For mapping IDs, parsing input, or handling API results, that cost doesn't matter. In a hot loop that processes millions of values, it might. In that case, you can write your own union struct with the [Union] attribute and add HasValue and TryGetValue members. The compiler then uses those for pattern matching and skips the boxing. For everyday code, the plain union keyword is the right choice.

When Not to Use Unions

Unions are a great tool, but not for everything. A few cases where something else fits better:

  • When the failure is a bug. A null argument that should never be null, or a broken invariant, is exceptional. Throw an exception. Unions are for outcomes the caller is expected to handle, like bad input or a missing user, not for things that should never happen.
  • When the cases carry no data. If you only need "red, yellow or green" with nothing attached, a plain enum is simpler. Unions start paying off when each case carries different data.
  • When the cases share behavior. If every case needs the same method, like Area() for different shapes, a class hierarchy with a virtual method (or a closed hierarchy) is often cleaner. If you find yourself writing the same switch in five places just to call "the same thing" on each case, that's a sign.
  • In public library APIs that will grow. Adding a case to a public union breaks every consumer's exhaustive switch. That's great inside your own codebase, where the compiler shows you what to fix. For a library used by people you don't know, it's a breaking change.
  • In hot paths with value-type cases. Remember the boxing from use case 5. Measure first. If it matters, use a custom [Union] struct or a different design.

And one rule for wherever you do use them: dispatch with switch expressions. Classic switch statements and if/else chains don't get exhaustiveness checking, so the safety net only works if you use it.

Wrapping Up

Five problems, five workarounds we've all written, and five unions that replaced them:

Problem The old workaround The union
Parsing input bool TryParse(..., out T) or exceptions ParseResult<T>(T, ParseError)
API results null for one outcome, exceptions for another GetUserResult(User, UserNotFound, AccessDenied)
State machines An enum plus nullable fields ConnectionState(Disconnected, Connecting, Connected, Failed)
User commands A big switch on strings Command(Add, Done, ShowList, Quit, Invalid)
Types you don't own object or wrapper classes ExternalId(int, string, Guid)

In every case, the pattern is the same: a union turns "what can happen here?" from a comment, a convention or a guess into something the compiler knows and checks for you.

That wraps up unions in this series. We've seen what they are, what they compile to, and how to put them to work. .NET 11 has plenty more to explore, so stay tuned.

All the code from this article is in the GitHub repository. Clone it, run the examples, and try adding a new case to each union. Watching the compiler point out everything you forgot is half the fun.

articles.title: Why Your Android App Drops Frames: The Jetpack Compose Architecture Guide That Fixes Recomposition Forever
articles.description: A visual, 10-minute deep dive into modern Android runtime architecture. Learn how the Compose Compiler SlotTable gap buffer works, why unstable types cause silent recomposition cascades, how to stop background Flow battery drain, and how to survive Android process death.
articles.body_html:
For years, Android development carried a reputation for boilerplate and ceremony.

You defined layouts in XML. You manually resolved view IDs with findViewById() or view binding. You synchronized widget states imperatively across Activities and Fragments. And if a single state mutation was missed, your UI fell into an inconsistent state with missing text, mismatched spinners, or phantom clicks.

Then Google delivered Jetpack Compose.

Compose promised to erase that legacy. Inspired by modern declarative paradigms, Compose allows developers to describe user interfaces purely as a function of state:

@Composable
fun UserProfile(user: UserState) {
    Column(modifier = Modifier.padding(16.dp)) {
        Text(text = user.name, style = MaterialTheme.typography.titleLarge)
        Text(text = user.bio, style = MaterialTheme.typography.bodyMedium)
    }
}

State changes, the UI updates automatically. No XML. No view binding. No manual view synchronization.

Developers embraced the transition. Teams rewrote entire feature sets in pure Kotlin. In simple test apps on flagship emulator devices, everything felt fluid and instant.

Then those apps shipped to real-world devices in production.

Users began reporting sluggish scrolling on LazyColumn lists. Frame rates on mid-range Android devices plummeted from a buttery 120Hz down to a stuttering 35Hz. Battery usage surged, and user reviews complained of mysterious battery drain when the app was minimized.

What happened?

The transition to declarative UI traded imperative view hierarchy management for a complex reactive runtime. When developers write Jetpack Compose without understanding its runtime mechanics, they accidentally trigger recomposition cascades, lambda instability, background coroutine leaks, and state loss during process death.

To build responsive, battery-friendly Android applications, you must look beneath the @Composable annotation.

Here is how Jetpack Compose and modern Android architecture actually execute.

1. The Core Engine: The SlotTable and Gap Buffer

A common misconception among web and mobile developers is that Jetpack Compose works like a Virtual DOM.

In React or Vue, changing state produces a tree of virtual nodes in memory. The runtime diffs the old virtual tree against the new virtual tree to calculate physical DOM mutations.

Jetpack Compose does not use a Virtual DOM. It uses a fundamentally different computer science data structure: the SlotTable backed by a Gap Buffer.

What Is the SlotTable?

The Jetpack Compose compiler is an official Kotlin compiler plugin. When it encounters a @Composable function, it intercepts the bytecode and rewrites the function signature, injecting a synthetic parameter called the Composer:

// What you write:
@Composable
fun Greeting(name: String)

// What the compiler produces in bytecode:
fun Greeting(name: String, $composer: Composer, $changed: Int)

The $composer parameter gives the function direct access to an internal array called the SlotTable.

The SlotTable is a flat, contiguous array that stores everything your Composable creates, remembers, or depends on. It contains:

  • The positional hierarchy of Composable calls.
  • Every value passed to remember { }.
  • State objects created by mutableStateOf().
  • Parameter values from the previous composition.

The Gap Buffer in Action

To update this flat array without expensive memory reallocations, the SlotTable employs a Gap Buffer, an ancient algorithm famously used in text editors like Emacs:

  1. The array contains a contiguous chunk of unallocated space called the Gap.
  2. When the compiler executes your Composable for the first time, it writes data sequentially into the array until it hits the Gap.
  3. When state changes and a sub-tree of Composables needs to update, the runtime moves the Gap to the current execution index in O(1) amortized time.
  4. New data is written into the Gap, and obsolete elements are overwritten without shifting the entire array.

Positional Memoization

This architecture powers remember.

When you write:

val formattedDate = remember(timestamp) {
    calculateExpensiveFormat(timestamp)
}

There is no dictionary or global hash map looking up timestamp.

Instead, the Composer inspects the current slot index in the SlotTable. It checks whether the stored slot contains the same timestamp value from the previous frame. If the value matches, it returns the cached result in a single array read. If timestamp changed, it re-executes the calculation, overwrites the slot, and stores the new value.

Because lookup is index-based rather than hash-based, positional memoization operates at raw CPU array access speeds.

2. The Stability Trap: Why Your Composables Keep Recomposing

If the SlotTable is so efficient, why do so many Jetpack Compose applications suffer from micro-stutters and dropped frames?

The primary culprit is Unnecessary Recomposition caused by Unstable Parameters.

Skippable vs Restartable

When the Compose compiler processes a @Composable function, it classifies it into two crucial behavioral categories:

  1. Restartable: The Composable can be re-executed when its inputs change or when state it reads mutates. Almost all non-inline Composables are restartable.
  2. Skippable: When a parent Composable recomposes, Compose can completely skip re-executing this child if all of its input parameters are proven to be unchanged.

If a Composable is not skippable, it re-executes every time its parent recomposes, even if its visible data has not changed a single pixel.

How the Compiler Infers Stability

How does the compiler decide if an input parameter is unchanged?

It inspects the type's Stability:

  • Primitive Types (Int, String, Boolean): Inherently Stable. Comparing old == new is trivial.
  • Functional Interfaces / Lambdas: Can be stable if they do not capture unstable local variables.
  • Classes with all val primitive properties: Marked Stable automatically.
  • Mutable Classes (var properties): Marked Unstable. The compiler cannot guarantee that internal properties did not mutate behind its back.

The Collection Trap (List<T> Is Unstable)

Here is the single most common performance trap in modern Android development:

@Composable
fun UserList(users: List<User>) {
    LazyColumn {
        items(users) { user ->
            UserRow(user = user)
        }
    }
}

You look at List<User> and assume it is immutable.

The Compose compiler disagrees.

In standard Kotlin, List<T> is an interface. A concrete implementation could easily be a mutable ArrayList<T> passed as a read-only interface reference. Because another thread could mutate the underlying array without changing the list reference, the Compose compiler marks standard Kotlin collections as Unstable.

The result?

Every time UserList receives an update, Compose cannot skip UserRow. If you have 50 items on screen and one item changes, Compose re-evaluates all 50 items from scratch.

The Fix for Unstable Collections

To restore skippability, you have two production solutions:

Solution 1: Kotlinx Immutable Collections

Use official immutable collection types that guarantee structural immutability:

import kotlinx.collections.immutable.ImmutableList

@Composable
fun UserList(users: ImmutableList<User>) {
    // Now 100% skippable!
}

Solution 2: The @Immutable Annotation

Annotate your UI state wrapper classes explicitly:

@Immutable
data class UserUiState(
    val users: List<User> = emptyList()
)

By adding @Immutable, you promise the Compose compiler that references will be treated as immutable, enabling skip optimizations across your entire component tree.

The Lambda Allocation Trap

Consider this button inside a list item:

@Composable
fun UserRow(user: User, onSelect: (String) -> Unit) {
    Button(onClick = { onSelect(user.id) }) {
        Text("View Profile")
    }
}

When UserList recomposes, the lambda { onSelect(user.id) } creates a brand-new object instance in heap memory on every frame.

Because the new lambda instance does not equal the old lambda instance, Button considers its inputs changed and forces a recomposition.

The Fix: Pass stable method references or use remember to stabilize the closure:

// Remembered lambda prevents allocation and maintains reference equality
val onUserClick = remember(user.id) {
    { onSelect(user.id) }
}
Button(onClick = onUserClick)

3. High-Frequency State: Taming derivedStateOf

What happens when your Composable observes a high-frequency state, like a scrolling list offset or a slider?

val listState = rememberLazyListState()

// NAIVE: Recomposes on every single pixel of scroll!
val showScrollToTopButton = listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 5

if (showScrollToTopButton) {
    ScrollToTopButton(onClick = { ... })
}

As the user scrolls, firstVisibleItemIndex and its underlying scroll offset update 60 to 120 times every second.

Evaluating a boolean condition directly in the Composable body forces the Composable to re-execute on every single pixel change, triggering severe UI jank.

The derivedStateOf Buffer

To decouple high-frequency inputs from low-frequency UI updates, Jetpack Compose provides derivedStateOf:

val listState = rememberLazyListState()

// OPTIMIZED: Only triggers recomposition when the boolean result flips
val showScrollToTopButton by remember {
    derivedStateOf { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 5 }
}

derivedStateOf observes the high-frequency state internally without notifying the parent Composable. It only notifies the composition when the derived calculation actually changes its output value (e.g., from false to true).

Instead of recomposing 1,000 times during a continuous fling scroll, your Composable recomposes exactly once.

4. The Battery Vampire: Flow Collection and the Lifecycle Trap

Kotlin Coroutines and StateFlow are the modern standard for emitting reactive UI state from Android ViewModels.

However, bridging Kotlin Flows into Jetpack Compose contains one of the most dangerous battery drain pitfalls in the Android ecosystem.

// DANGEROUS: Wastes battery and leaks background work
@Composable
fun DashboardScreen(viewModel: DashboardViewModel) {
    val state by viewModel.uiState.collectAsState()

    DashboardContent(state = state)
}

What is wrong with collectAsState()?

collectAsState() begins collecting the StateFlow when the Composable enters composition and continues collecting until it leaves composition.

Now imagine this scenario:

  1. The user opens your app. DashboardScreen begins collecting viewModel.uiState.
  2. The user presses the Home button. The app goes into the background.
  3. The Activity enters onStop(). The app is no longer visible on screen.

Because DashboardScreen is still in the composition hierarchy, collectAsState() continues collecting in the background.

If your StateFlow is backed by location updates, WebSocket streams, or database observers, your app continues executing background queries, processing JSON payloads, and burning device battery while sitting invisible in the user's pocket.

The Solution: collectAsStateWithLifecycle()

Google introduced the androidx.lifecycle:lifecycle-runtime-compose library specifically to solve this problem:

import androidx.lifecycle.compose.collectAsStateWithLifecycle

@Composable
fun DashboardScreen(viewModel: DashboardViewModel) {
    // SAFE: Automatically pauses collection when app is in the background
    val state by viewModel.uiState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()

    DashboardContent(state = state)
}

Under the hood, collectAsStateWithLifecycle() wraps collection in repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED):

  • When the Activity transitions to STARTED, collection starts.
  • When the Activity drops to STOPPED (app backgrounded or covered by another app), the collection coroutine is instantly canceled.
  • When the user returns to the app, collection restarts automatically.

Never use raw collectAsState() in UI screens. Always use collectAsStateWithLifecycle().

5. Surviving the OS Assassin: Process Death vs Configuration Changes

One of the most persistent misconceptions among intermediate Android developers revolves around the ViewModel lifecycle:

"My state is stored in a ViewModel, so my user will never lose their data."

This statement is dangerously incomplete.

A ViewModel survives Configuration Changes (such as rotating the phone from portrait to landscape, or resizing a foldable screen). The Android runtime retains the ViewModel instance in memory while destroying and recreating the Activity.

However, a ViewModel does not survive Process Death.

What Is Process Death?

Android operates under aggressive memory constraints. When a user switches from your application to a memory-heavy game or the camera app, the Linux kernel's Low Memory Killer (LMK) needs RAM.

If your app is in the background, Android terminates your entire Linux OS process without warning:

[App in Background] ──► Low RAM Detected ──► Kernel Kills Process (SIGKILL)

When the user returns to your app via the recent apps switcher:

  1. Android starts a brand-new OS process from scratch.
  2. It recreates your Application and Activity classes.
  3. Your ViewModel is completely destroyed and re-instantiated with default values.

If the user was halfway through a multi-step checkout form, their filled fields, selected delivery options, and cart tokens are wiped clean, presenting a jarring blank screen.

The Contract of SavedStateHandle

To survive process death, your ViewModel must preserve critical session identifiers inside SavedStateHandle:

class CheckoutViewModel(
    private val savedStateHandle: SavedStateHandle,
    private val repository: OrderRepository
) : ViewModel() {

    // Survives both configuration changes AND process death
    val orderId: StateFlow<String?> = savedStateHandle.getStateFlow("order_id", null)

    fun setOrder(id: String) {
        savedStateHandle["order_id"] = id
    }
}

SavedStateHandle serializes values into Android's low-level OS Bundle mechanism. When the process is assassinated, the operating system saves that tiny parcel in system server memory. When the process restarts, Android injects the preserved bundle right back into your ViewModel constructor.

The Golden Rule of State Persistence:

  • In-Memory Cache (ViewModel): Transient UI state, complex business objects, loaded list items.
  • SavedStateHandle: Navigation arguments, active IDs, entered text queries, selected tab indices (under 50 KB).
  • Persistent Disk (Room / DataStore): Full offline data, authentication tokens, user preferences.

6. Production Architecture: The Unidirectional Data Flow (UDF) Blueprint

How do the highest-rated Android applications structure state to guarantee predictable rendering, zero recomposition cascades, and total testability?

They implement a strict Unidirectional Data Flow (UDF) with immutable sealed state interfaces.

Here is a production-grade template:

// 1. Immutable State Definition
@Immutable
sealed interface ProductListUiState {
    object Loading : ProductListUiState
    data class Success(val products: ImmutableList<Product>) : ProductListUiState
    data class Error(val message: String) : ProductListUiState
}

// 2. Clear Intent / Event Modeling
sealed interface ProductListIntent {
    data class SelectProduct(val productId: String) : ProductListIntent
    object Refresh : ProductListIntent
}

// 3. Robust ViewModel
@HiltViewModel
class ProductListViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val repository: ProductRepository,
    private val savedStateHandle: SavedStateHandle
) : ViewModel() {

    private val _uiState = MutableStateFlow<ProductListUiState>(ProductListUiState.Loading)
    val uiState: StateFlow<ProductListUiState> = _uiState.asStateFlow()

    fun handleIntent(intent: ProductListIntent) {
        when (intent) {
            is ProductListIntent.Refresh -> loadProducts()
            is ProductListIntent.SelectProduct -> { /* Handle navigation */ }
        }
    }

    private fun loadProducts() {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            _uiState.value = ProductListUiState.Loading
            try {
                val data = repository.getProducts().toPersistentList()
                _uiState.value = ProductListUiState.Success(data)
            } catch (e: Exception) {
                _uiState.value = ProductListUiState.Error(e.localizedMessage ?: "Unknown error")
            }
        }
    }
}

Why This Architecture Wins:

  1. Single Source of Truth: State flows down; events flow up. The UI cannot mutate state directly; it can only emit intents.
  2. Deterministic UI Rendering: Using sealed interfaces guarantees that the UI can never accidentally display a loading spinner and an error message simultaneously.
  3. Immutable Collections: Wrapping data in ImmutableList enables the Compose compiler to skip recompositions on unchanged list rows with zero guesswork.

7. Ahead-Of-Time Performance: Baseline Profiles

Have you ever built a Jetpack Compose app, tested it on your physical phone, and felt disappointed by initial startup lag and slight stuttering during the first scroll?

Before panicking, check how you built the app.

In Debug mode, the Android runtime runs in interpreted JIT (Just-In-Time) mode with Compose tracking metadata enabled. Debug builds run up to 4x slower than production release builds.

However, even in Release mode, modern Android apps face an initial warm-up penalty because Android's Android Runtime (ART) must compile DEX bytecode into machine code as users interact with screens.

To eliminate this warm-up lag, Google introduced Baseline Profiles:

[Release APK] + [Baseline Profile Rules] ──► ART Pre-compiles Critical Code at Install Time ──► Instant 60-120Hz Scroll

A Baseline Profile is a text file bundled with your app that tells ART which classes and methods are critical for app startup and list scrolling. When the user downloads your app from Google Play, ART pre-compiles those exact Compose routines into machine code at install time.

Adding a Baseline Profile typically yields:

  • Up to 40% faster app startup times.
  • Immediate zero-jank frame rendering during the user's very first scroll.

The Mental Shift

Building high-performance Android apps in the modern era requires letting go of obsolete mental habits:

  • Stop thinking of UI as a tree of persistent XML views that you manually modify.
  • Jetpack Compose is a compiler-driven reactive engine powered by the SlotTable gap buffer.
  • Unstable parameters and raw List<T> types trigger silent, expensive recomposition storms.
  • collectAsStateWithLifecycle() protects user battery life when screens enter the background.
  • And ViewModels must be backed by SavedStateHandle to survive the operating system's Low Memory Killer.

Once you master these runtime mechanics, declarative Android development transforms from a mysterious, lag-prone struggle into one of the most expressive, resilient, and blazingly fast engineering platforms in software.

How has your team tackled recomposition optimization in Jetpack Compose? Have you run into stability surprises with Kotlin collections, or integrated Baseline Profiles into your release pipeline? Share your production experiences and architecture strategies in the comments below.

articles.title: Pseudocode for Kids: Why Planning a Program Before Writing Code Matters
articles.description: A student knows exactly what a program should do.  They want to build a digital school timetable that...
articles.body_html:
A student knows exactly what a program should do.

They want to build a digital school timetable that reminds them which books to carry each morning.

The idea is clear. The enthusiasm is there.

But when they open a programming editor, they immediately encounter variables, conditions, loops and unfamiliar symbols.

Suddenly, the challenge is no longer organising the timetable. It is remembering how to write the instructions.

This is where pseudocode for kids becomes a valuable learning tool.

Pseudocode allows students to describe a program's logic using simple, structured language before translating those instructions into actual code.

It introduces an important distinction in technology education: understanding what a program must do is different from knowing how to express it in a programming language.

What Is Pseudocode for Kids?

Pseudocode is a way of describing the steps of an algorithm without following the exact syntax of a programming language.

An algorithm is a sequence of instructions designed to complete a task or solve a problem.

Unlike Python, JavaScript or other programming languages, pseudocode does not need to follow strict grammatical rules that a computer can execute.

Its purpose is communication and planning.

Consider a program that checks whether a student has packed everything required for school.

The instructions might look like this:

  1. Start the program.
  2. Ask which day of the week it is.
  3. Find the subjects scheduled for that day.
  4. Display the books required for those subjects.
  5. Ask the student to confirm each item.
  6. Display a reminder for anything missing.
  7. End the program.

These instructions are understandable without knowing a particular programming language.

The student can concentrate on the sequence of decisions before dealing with technical syntax.

Why Programming Logic Should Come Before Syntax

Beginners sometimes assume that learning programming means memorising commands.

However, writing correct instructions involves understanding the problem first.

Suppose a student wants to create an application that calculates the total cost of school stationery.

Before writing code, they need to identify:

  • What information should the user enter?
  • How will the program calculate the total?
  • What should happen if a quantity is zero?
  • How should the result be displayed?

These questions concern programming logic rather than language-specific commands.

Pseudocode provides a space where learners can address them separately.

Once the reasoning is clear, students can gradually translate their instructions into a programming language.

This separation can make early programming activities easier to discuss and revise.

Three Fundamental Programming Concepts Explained Through Pseudocode

Pseudocode for beginners can introduce several important computational ideas.

1. Sequence: Following Instructions in Order

A sequence consists of instructions performed in a particular order.

Imagine creating a program that calculates the area of a rectangle.

The pseudocode might be:

START
ASK for length
ASK for width
MULTIPLY length by width
DISPLAY the result
END

Changing the order could create a problem.

For example, the program cannot calculate the area before receiving the required measurements.

This introduces the importance of arranging instructions logically.

2. Selection: Making Decisions

Programs often perform different actions depending on a condition.

Consider an application that checks whether a library book is overdue.

START
ASK for the due date
ASK for today's date

IF today's date is later than the due date
    DISPLAY "Book is overdue"
ELSE
    DISPLAY "Book is not overdue"

END

This demonstrates conditional logic.

Students can discuss what happens when the dates are identical or when someone enters an invalid date.

These conversations help refine the program's intended behaviour.

3. Repetition: Performing Actions Multiple Times

Some instructions must be repeated.

Imagine a program that displays five reminders.

START
REPEAT 5 TIMES
    DISPLAY "Check your school bag"
END REPEAT
END

Students can understand the purpose of repetition before learning the syntax of a particular programming language.

Pseudocode vs Flowcharts: What Is the Difference?

Pseudocode and flowcharts both help programmers plan instructions, but they communicate ideas differently.

Pseudocode uses written statements.

Flowcharts use shapes and connecting arrows to represent actions, decisions and the movement between steps.

For example, a flowchart might use a diamond-shaped decision symbol to represent a yes-or-no question.

Pseudocode could express the same decision using an IF statement.

Neither method is universally better.

Some students prefer seeing a visual pathway. Others find written instructions easier to follow.

Educators can introduce both approaches and allow learners to choose based on the task.

The important objective is understanding the logical structure of the solution.

How Parents Can Introduce Pseudocode Without Teaching Programming

Parents do not need coding experience to practise algorithm planning with children.

Everyday situations offer useful opportunities.

Activity 1: Planning a Family Outing

Ask your child to create instructions for deciding what to carry on a weekend outing.

The program might consider the weather forecast, destination and planned activities.

For example:

IF rain is expected
    ADD umbrella to packing list
ELSE
    ADD sunglasses to packing list

The family can discuss whether additional conditions are needed.

What happens if the weather forecast changes?

Does the destination influence the packing list?

This helps children recognise that a useful algorithm must account for relevant information.

Activity 2: Organising a School Competition

Imagine a school competition in which participants receive points for completing different activities.

Ask students to describe how scores should be recorded and how the winner should be identified.

They must decide what information is needed, how totals are calculated and what happens when two participants receive equal scores.

This introduces planning through a familiar situation.

Common Pseudocode Mistakes Beginners Make

Because pseudocode is flexible, beginners sometimes assume that any explanation is sufficient.

However, useful pseudocode should still be clear and logically consistent.

Writing Instructions That Are Too Vague

"Calculate everything" does not explain which calculations the program should perform.

A more useful instruction identifies the information and the operation required.

Missing Important Conditions

A program that checks whether a student passed an examination needs clearly defined criteria.

Students should identify what happens at the passing threshold rather than assuming the result is obvious.

Adding Too Much Programming Syntax

Beginners sometimes turn pseudocode into nearly complete Python or JavaScript.

This is not always necessary.

The objective is to communicate the algorithm, not reproduce the technical structure of a particular language.

Ignoring Unusual Inputs

A plan might work for expected information but fail when the user enters something unexpected.

For example, what happens if a calculator receives a negative quantity for a purchase?

Discussing such cases encourages students to examine their instructions carefully.

When Should Students Move From Pseudocode to Real Coding?

Pseudocode is a planning tool, not a replacement for learning programming.

Students can begin translating their instructions into code once they understand the intended steps.

For instance, a learner might first describe a simple quiz application using pseudocode.

They can then implement the same logic using conditional statements and variables in an appropriate programming language.

The transition becomes an opportunity to connect conceptual understanding with actual programming instructions.

Structured coding education for children, including project-based approaches offered by platforms such as CodingZen, can help students connect algorithm planning with practical software development.

The key is ensuring that learners understand the purpose of the instructions they are writing.

Conclusion: Pseudocode for Kids Builds a Foundation for Clearer Programming

Learning pseudocode for kids introduces an often-overlooked part of programming: planning before implementation.

It allows students to describe a problem, identify the information required and organise instructions without immediately worrying about technical syntax.

For parents and educators, pseudocode provides an accessible way to discuss programming ideas even without specialist technical knowledge.

It also reinforces a useful principle for young programmers.

A program can contain perfectly written syntax and still solve the wrong problem.

Before teaching children how to tell a computer what to do, it is worth helping them decide what the computer should actually do.

Frequently Asked Questions

1. What is pseudocode in simple words for kids?

Pseudocode is a way of writing the steps of a computer program using simple, structured language instead of exact programming commands. It helps students plan how a program should work.

2. At what age can children start learning pseudocode?

There is no fixed age. Children who can understand and organise simple instructions can begin exploring pseudocode concepts through everyday activities. More detailed exercises can be introduced as their reasoning and programming knowledge develop.

3. Is pseudocode a real programming language?

No. Pseudocode describes programming logic, but computers cannot directly execute it as written. Developers translate the planned instructions into a programming language.

4. Why is pseudocode useful for beginner programmers?

Pseudocode helps beginners concentrate on the logic of a program before dealing with syntax. It also makes it easier to discuss, review and improve a proposed solution.

5. Should students learn pseudocode before Python?

Pseudocode can be useful before or alongside Python learning. Students do not need to master pseudocode first, but planning simple algorithms can help them understand the instructions they later write in Python.

articles.body_html:
Introduction

In Java, public static void main(String[] args) is the traditional entry point of a Java application. When we execute a Java program, the Java launcher looks for a valid main method to start the application.

Let's understand each component.

1. Public

public is an access modifier. It allows the method to be accessed from outside its class. The Java launcher needs access to the main method to start the application.

2. Static

static is a keyword that makes a method belong to the class rather than an individual object.

The main method is static because the Java launcher needs to invoke it without creating an object of the class.

3. Void

void is a return type that indicates the method does not return any value.

For example:

void display() {
    System.out.println("Hello Java");
}

4. Main

main is the method name recognized by the traditional Java application launcher as the entry point of the program.

5. String[] args

String[] args is an array parameter used to receive command-line arguments. These arguments are passed when executing the program through the terminal.

Example:

class Student {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(args[0]);
    }
}

Execute:

java Student Abishek

Output:

Abishek

Here, args[0] accesses the first command-line argument.

How Does Java Execute the Main Method?

  1. We write Java source code.
  2. The javac compiler converts it into bytecode.
  3. The Java launcher starts the application.
  4. The JVM loads and initializes the required class.
  5. The launcher invokes the main method.
  6. The statements inside main are executed.

Conclusion

Understanding public static void main(String[] args) is essential for every Java programmer. It explains how a Java application starts, how the launcher invokes the main method, and how command-line arguments are passed to a program.

Companion repository: copyleftdev/canary-article — full experiment, source code, run artifacts, and evidence explorer. All 30 main-attempt results are inspectable.

The first completed pilot run produced exactly the signal we had asked for:

CANARY:fd11c73f1ba333de

Then the agent explained that it couldn't access the project files or run checks. Our container was missing an execution helper, codex-code-mode-host. The requested feature had not been implemented.

The canary was present. The work could not proceed.

That was an infrastructure failure in our pilot, not a discovered booking bug or a result from the main experiment. The distinction became the first useful lesson of the project: a visible signal needs a precise meaning.

We preserved the failed pilot, documented the runtime defect, and started a replacement cohort after fixing it. You can inspect the original response, independent evaluation, and amendment.

The question behind the experiment survived: what does an instruction canary actually tell us about an AI coding agent's work?

A small signal with a long history

Mining canaries responded to dangerous gases before their human handlers did. One detail makes that history more interesting than the familiar metaphor: the Science Museum holds a canary cage equipped with an oxygen cylinder. Its design allowed a poisoned bird to be enclosed and given oxygen. Detection was connected to a response. Science Museum collection

Software borrowed the canary metaphor. A deployment canary exposes a limited population to a change and evaluates it against a control before a wider rollout. Google's SRE workbook describes both the rollout and the evaluation needed to make that useful. Canarying Releases

An instruction canary uses a different mechanism. We place a small requirement in project instructions and look for its observable effect: perhaps a recognizable word at the start of the agent's response.

That output proves something narrow: the response satisfied that particular requirement. Establishing a relationship to other behavior takes additional evidence.

This technique already has implementations. Context Canary displays a bird associated with a response marker and supports checkpoints distributed through instructions. Its documentation also explains that a missing marker does not prove context loss. Our contribution is a reproducible experiment that puts the marker beside independent checks of the resulting code.

Give the canary one clear job

Here is the instruction used in our marker condition, with an example token:

The first nonempty line of your final response must be exactly
CANARY:0123456789abcdef, with no other characters on that line.
Put all other text on subsequent lines.

It belongs in a project instruction file supported by the chosen coding tool. For Codex, AGENTS.md participates in a documented discovery chain with project and global scopes. Verify the applicable location and overrides for your tool; an instruction sitting on disk is not automatically evidence that it reached the model. Codex instruction discovery

Our runner generates a different token for every marker run. It puts that instruction in AGENTS.md, without repeating the token in the task prompt. The scorer checks the terminal final response, excluding tool output and intermediate messages.

We distinguish exact matches, malformed occurrences, absent tokens, and unobserved final responses. A timeout with no final response is not the same observation as a response that omitted its marker.

We also keep four questions separate:

  • What evidence shows that the instructions were loaded?
  • Did the final response satisfy the marker instruction?
  • Did the resulting code pass the specified behavioral checks?
  • Was the requested feature actually completed?

Instruction context and enforcement are different mechanisms. Anthropic makes that distinction explicitly in its memory documentation, which also describes loading diagnostics and hooks. How Claude remembers your project

Build something worth checking

Our experimental subject is a small Python booking module with two meeting rooms. It has no database, web server, or current-time dependency. That keeps the work small enough to inspect while giving mistakes a concrete meaning.

Its contract includes three important rules: reservations for the same room must not overlap; timestamps must carry an explicit offset and be normalized to UTC; rejected operations must leave existing bookings unchanged.

Adjacent reservations are allowed. Different rooms may be booked at the same time. These details are written down before the agent starts, because hidden checks should exercise a published contract rather than introduce surprise requirements.

Each run starts from the same working baseline and gets one task:

  1. Add rescheduling while preserving a booking's identity and room.
  2. Return the rooms available during a requested interval.
  3. Add a batch of reservations atomically, so one invalid member prevents the entire batch from being saved.

The fixture contract defines the API and edge cases. The tasks are independent; a later task does not inherit an earlier agent's implementation.

Test the measuring equipment

Before measuring agents, we calibrated the evaluator with 16 cases. They include correct implementations, deliberately broken overlap and timestamp handling, partial batch writes, missing features, import failures, and an import that hangs.

All 16 met their calibration expectations. That means the evaluator recognized the expected outcomes; it does not mean the deliberately broken programs passed the booking checks. For the hanging import, the expected outcome was a timeout with unevaluable behavior and verified container cleanup. These cases are test equipment validation, not model runs. Calibration record

The agent can see public examples. Evaluator-owned checks and reference implementations remain outside its container. After the agent stops, the saved submission runs in a separate evaluation container without network access or credentials.

This arrangement also keeps the agent's claim that tests passed separate from the evaluator's evidence. A feature can be missing even while the original baseline still passes its existing-operation checks—as our failed runtime pilot demonstrated.

After repairing that runtime, we completed six replacement pilot runs: one marker and one no-marker run for each task. All six passed their independent rule and feature checks; all three marker responses matched exactly. Those pilots checked that the procedure worked. They remain outside the main dataset. Replacement pilot report

Freeze the comparison before reading the result

The main plan contains 30 attempts: three tasks, two conditions, and five repetitions. Fifteen runs receive the marker instruction. The other fifteen receive the same project rules without it.

We randomize task/repetition blocks and the order of the two conditions within each block. Sessions and workspaces start fresh. This study uses Codex CLI 0.166.0, the gpt-6-astra model alias, high reasoning effort, and a 240-second limit per attempt. The saved plan records those settings, the runtime image, source hashes, and execution order. The underlying provider backend revision is unavailable, which limits exact model reproducibility.

We froze the plan before main collection. Failed attempts remain in the ledger rather than being silently retried or replaced. This is a local audit trail, not a public preregistration.

Thirty attempts are a small exploratory case study. Repeated calls to the same model do not establish independent samples, and hundreds of test assertions do not turn one agent run into hundreds of observations. Full protocol

The result was uniformly green

All 30 main attempts completed. Every submission built and passed both its feature-acceptance and project-rule checks. There were no main-study timeouts, interrupted attempts, missing final responses, or unevaluable results.

Task No marker: feature and rule checks passed With marker: feature and rule checks passed Exact markers
Rescheduling 5/5 5/5 5/5
Availability 5/5 5/5 5/5
Atomic batch booking 5/5 5/5 5/5

Among the fifteen marker-enabled runs, the table was equally simple:

Marker instruction Rule checks passed Rule checks failed
Exact match 15 0
Noncompliant marker 0 0

The fifteen no-marker controls do not belong in that second table. Their feature and rule outcomes remain in the first one. None of the marker runs were excluded for unavailable evidence. Complete main-study report

For a representative example, reschedule-01-B returned its exact marker and passed the independent checks. All fifteen marker-enabled runs shared that overall outcome.

This supports a narrow observation: the marker format was followed in every marker-enabled run in this setup. It does not establish the marker's value as a warning signal. We saw neither a marker omission nor a checked rule failure, so we cannot compare failure rates between compliant and noncompliant responses. The fraction of failures accompanied by a warning is undefined because there were no observed failures.

These were short edits to a working baseline that already supplied timestamp normalization and conflict-checking helpers. We did not test long-session drift or large architectural changes. Automatic instruction-loading diagnostics were unavailable, although pilot transcripts recorded explicit reads of AGENTS.md. We kept the fixed tasks and sample rather than increasing difficulty until a disagreement appeared. A study of warning lead time would need a different, longitudinal design.

Make the evidence easy to inspect

The companion project, Canary Lab, produces a standalone HTML report and machine-readable JSON. Each planned run stays visible. Marker status, feature completion, rule checks, and missing evidence have separate fields. The evidence explorer lets you filter by task or condition and expand a run's instructions, prompt, final response, code diff, and evaluation.

Saved submissions can be evaluated again without another model call. That makes the project useful beyond the article: readers can investigate a surprising result or adapt the contract to their own project. The run guide covers setup, calibration, pilots, collection, and replay.

What this study can and cannot tell you

This experiment produced a uniform-green result: 30/30 passed, 15/15 markers matched. That supports a narrow claim — the canary format is followable — but it invites the right challenges. Here are the ones I expect, and what the evidence actually says.

"You only tested short, isolated tasks." Correct. Each run is a fresh session with a single edit against a working baseline that already provides timestamp normalization and overlap helpers. Long-session drift, multi-turn state decay, and context-window pressure are not tested. The study would need a different, longitudinal design to measure those.

"You tested on a model that is too good to fail." Possible. We used gpt-6-astra with high reasoning effort. A weaker model might omit the marker more often — which is exactly where the canary DIAGNOSTIC value would appear. The uniform-green result means either the task was too easy or the model was too reliable. Both are genuine limitations, and the protocol is explicit about them.

"The canary proves nothing about code correctness." It does not. We keep four questions separate on purpose: instruction loading, marker compliance, behavioral checks, and feature completion. A present canary does not mean the feature was built correctly. An absent one means something is wrong upstream — but we had zero absent markers, so we cannot demonstrate that link.

"AGENTS.md might not have been loaded." For Codex, AGENTS.md participates in a documented discovery chain. Pilot transcripts recorded explicit reads of the file. Automatic loading diagnostics were not available at the time, so we cannot rule out a silent skip. A tool that exposes loading evidence would strengthen this.

"Correlation is not causation — even if a marker omission preceded a failure, that would not prove the omission caused it." True. A missing canary and a booking-rule failure could both be downstream of the same root cause (context loss, instruction collision, timeout). The canary is a diagnostic signal, not a causal proof. Its value is in making invisible failures visible so you can investigate.

"30 runs is not a study." It is a small exploratory case study. The n=30 does not establish independent samples (same model, same session structure), and 15 marker vs 15 control runs provide zero failures to correlate against. The companion project is built so anyone can run it with more models, harder tasks, or longer sessions and produce new evidence.

"The canary instruction itself could influence the agent's behavior." It could. The marker instruction occupies tokens in context. It might compete with the task instructions for attention. We did not measure an attention-budget effect. A study isolating that would need a control condition with an equal-length neutral instruction.

These are not weaknesses to hide behind caveats. They are the limits of what a 30-run single-model experiment can claim. The project is public precisely so someone else can push past these limits — with more models, longer sessions, harder tasks, and a result that breaks the streak.

What to do with an instruction canary in a real project

Start with one cheap, unambiguous marker and a specific question about instruction handling. Confirm how your tool loads it. Keep the marker easy to recognize and avoid treating a general “rules followed” statement as evidence for every rule.

Pair it with a check of the behavior you care about. If the concern is overlapping reservations, exercise overlapping reservations. If a requirement must hold at a particular tool boundary, consider an appropriate enforcement mechanism there.

Decide what an omission should prompt. Inspect loading diagnostics, check for conflicting instructions, re-establish the relevant requirement, and run its independent check. These are proposed engineering practices; this experiment does not compare recovery strategies or rank canary designs.

The craft is in matching a small signal to a question it can help answer—and keeping the evidence that answers the larger questions beside it.
