  • Upgrading
  • What's Next

A New CLI

stencil init scaffolds a project by asking what you need: output targets, a framework integration (like for React, Vue or Angular), a test runner, a CSS preprocessor. It installs and configures what you pick.

To add something later, run stencil add. It shows the same choices as init, and works with any participating package that ships its own setup wizard. So stencil add @stencil/vitest installs Vitest, guides you through a wizard and writes its config.

stencil migrate updates a v4 project. More on that below.

Four Kinds of Component

I feel like design systems need more than one kind of component. A badge might only need styles. A share link might be best as a slotted <a> that gets extra behaviour once JavaScript loads. A dropdown renders its own markup. A complex input might want shadow DOM, to keep its internals separate from the page.

Component Archetypes compares the four kinds of component you can build: CSS-only, progressively enhanced, custom elements without shadow DOM, and custom elements with it.

For any component requiring JavaScript, Stencil v5 has moved these options into a new encapsulation object:

// src/my-input.tsx

@Component({
  tag: 'my-input',
  encapsulation: { type: 'shadow' }, // or 'scoped', or 'none'
})

Left out, the component renders into the light DOM with no encapsulation (and components without shadow DOM still get <slot>s). scoped and none components can also pick / override which light DOM patches they need, per component.

v5 also introduces new globalStyle / globalStyleUrl properties on your component definition:

@Component({
  tag: 'my-input',
  style: `:host { display: block; }`,
  // ^ style your component internals after it's loaded
  globalStyle: `my-input { min-height: 20px; }`
  // ^ pre-style your component or its contents before it's loaded
  // to help with FOUC, CLS and progressive enhancement
})

Read more about co-locating styles with your components.

CSS-Only Components

When components don't need JavaScript at all (a badge, a divider, a layout grid), you can write one as a stylesheet. A /** @component */ comment turns a rule into a component:

/* src/my-badge.css */
/**
 * @component
 * A small label for a status or count.
 */
my-badge {
  /** The badge's background color. */
  --badge-color: #e0e0e0;
  display: inline-flex;
  background: var(--badge-color);

  /** Variant (the enum type attribute is auto-documented) */
  &[variant='success'] {
    --badge-color: #c8f0d0;
  }
  &[variant='danger'] {
    --badge-color: #f8d0d0;
  }

  /** Pill (the boolean type attribute is auto-documented) */
  &[pill] {
    border-radius: 999px;
  }

  /** Icon (slots are auto-documented) */
  > [slot='icon'] {
    width: 1em;
  }
}

<my-badge> is never registered as a custom element; there's no JS runtime to load. Stencil still adds it to your JSX types and generated docs, and ships its CSS with your global styles.

Thanks to Burton Smith's initial idea, I wholly agreed and went all-in!

New Shadow DOM Features

For components that do use shadow DOM, more of the platform's shadow root options are now supported.

Scoped custom element registries let two versions of a library define the same tag on one page, each in its own part of it. They now have first-class support - see Scoped Registries.

  • referenceTarget forwards a <label for> or aria-labelledby that points at your component to an element inside its shadow root (so far only Chromium-based browsers support this - Chrome and Edge 152+).
  • mode: 'closed' disables access to element.shadowRoot.
  • clonable keeps the shadow root when the host is deep-cloned with cloneNode(true) (otherwise you get an empty shell).
  • serializable includes the shadow root when the host is serialized with getHTML({ serializableShadowRoots: true }).
  • delegatesFocus and slotAssignment sit alongside them in the same object. 
@Component({
  tag: 'my-input',
  encapsulation: {
    type: 'shadow',
    referenceTarget: 'field',
    mode: 'closed',
    clonable: true,
  },
})
export class MyInput {
  render() {
    return <input id="field" />;
  }
}

Form-associated components no longer need a flag - using the @AttachInternals() decorator sets that up for you.

Signals

Stencil v5 includes Preact Signals. A signal holds a value outside any one component, so several components can share it. Put a signal in JSX and Stencil updates that one text node when it changes, without rendering the component again:

// src/count.ts

import { signal } from '@stencil/core/signals';

export const count = signal(0);

// src/my-counter.tsx

import { Component } from '@stencil/core';
import { count } from './count';

@Component({ tag: 'my-counter' })
export class MyCounter {
  render() {
    return <button onClick={() => count.value++}>{count}</button>;
  }
}

A new @Effect() decorator (also from @stencil/core/signals) runs a method again whenever a signal it reads changes.

Signal-Backed Components

Turn on signalBacking in your config and every @Prop() and @State() is stored in a signal too (you don't have to change your component code). This makes your components' props subscribable from outside. Other components and Preact Signals code can react to them directly, and frameworks can follow along without listening for events or watching attributes:

// my-app/src/doubled-volume.ts

import { getSignal, computed } from '@stencil/core/signals';

// <my-slider> has a `@Prop() value: number`
const sliderEl = document.querySelector('my-slider');
await sliderEl.componentOnReady();

const volume = getSignal<number>(sliderEl, 'value');
export const doubledVolume = computed(() => volume.value * 2);

The Signals guide has live examples.

Reactive Controllers

Stencil v5 now has much better interop with reactive controllers - reusable objects that hook into a component's lifecycle - without writing glue code. Mix ReactiveControllerHost into a component, and every controller you add gets hostConnected, hostWillRender, hostDidUpdate etc:

// src/mouse-controller.ts

import type { ReactiveController, ReactiveControllerHostInterface } from '@stencil/core';

export class MouseController implements ReactiveController {
  pos = { x: 0, y: 0 };

  constructor(private host: ReactiveControllerHostInterface) {
    host.addController(this);
  }

  private onMove = (e: MouseEvent) => {
    this.pos = { x: e.clientX, y: e.clientY };
    this.host.requestUpdate();
  };

  hostConnected() {
    window.addEventListener('mousemove', this.onMove);
  }

  hostDisconnected() {
    window.removeEventListener('mousemove', this.onMove);
  }
}

// src/my-mouse.tsx

import { Component, Host, Mixin, ReactiveControllerHost } from '@stencil/core';
import { MouseController } from './mouse-controller';

@Component({ tag: 'my-mouse' })
export class MyMouse extends Mixin(ReactiveControllerHost) {
  private mouse = new MouseController(this);

  render() {
    return <Host>{this.mouse.pos.x}, {this.mouse.pos.y}</Host>;
  }
}

See some more examples.

Styling

Global styles now get their own output target, global-style. You can have as many as you like (e.g. a separate light and dark theme) and choose, with inject, whether each one is also added to your shadow DOM components. Read more.

Add @import "stencil-hydrate"; to a global stylesheet and Stencil writes its FOUC-prevention CSS (hiding components until they've loaded) into that file at build time. This replaces the default behaviour of the loader injecting a <style> tag at runtime.

Less Boilerplate

v5 has removed a lot of the requirements around boilerplate, so a new, default project doesn't need:

  • A stencil.config.ts. With no config, Stencil builds a loader-bundle - the output most design systems want.
  • A namespace. It's taken from your package.json name (or the directory name).
  • A tsconfig.json. If there isn't one, Stencil writes one for you.
  • An index.html. The dev server generates preview pages for your components.
  • Global style / script wiring. src/global.{css,scss,sass} and src/global.{ts,js} are picked up automatically.

A folder of .tsx files and npx stencil build --dev --serve is enough to get going. Add config later if you need it.

Development Previews

We've added auto-previews to Stencil's built-in dev server.

Add examples to the usage folder (e.g. src/my-button/usage/basic.md), and their html code blocks become the preview. Run stencil build --dev --serve and navigate to the component's folder:

If you prefer granular control, continue using index.html files as you do now. Alternatively, we've made the integration with Storybook even nicer :)

Server-Side Rendering

The dist-hydrate-script output target is now ssr. The SSR examples repo has working setups for Next.js, React Router, TanStack Start, Nuxt, SvelteKit, SolidStart, Astro, Angular and Eleventy.

Streaming

SSR can now stream - streamToString() returns a web-standard ReadableStream, so it runs in Node, Cloudflare Workers, Deno, Bun and other edge runtimes.

SSR WASM

There's also the new (still a bit experimental) ssr-wasm output target. It compiles your server renderer to WebAssembly, so a server in PHP, Java, Go, .NET or any other language can render your components without Node.js. Check out the SSR WASM examples repo.

Using Your Components Elsewhere

We've added more outputs and supporting libraries, meaning your components can compile, run and be read in more ways.

  • Framework types. React 19, Vue, Solid, Svelte, Preact and Astro render custom elements without wrappers. @stencil/types-output-target generates the types that let them type-check your components' props and events.
  • The bundler plugin. @stencil/unplugin compiles Stencil components inside Vite, webpack, Rspack, Rollup or esbuild. Write components directly in an app, with no separate Stencil build. So far we mainly use it for Vitest and Storybook, but it may be useful elsewhere.
  • An agent skill. The docs-agent-skill output target generates a skill from your JSDoc comments and usage examples, so AI coding agents can use your library correctly.

Testing

Stencil's built-in test runner (stencil test --spec and --e2e, with Jest and Puppeteer) is gone. Its replacements are separate packages:

  • @stencil/vitest for unit and component tests, in Node or in real browsers.
  • @stencil/playwright for end-to-end tests across browsers.

Both have migration guides, and you can keep your existing newSpecPage() tests while you move.

Under the Hood

Builds are around 1.5–2× faster than v4 (benchmarks).

  • Rolldown. Stencil now bundles with Rolldown in place of Rollup. rollupConfig and rollupPlugins become rolldownConfig and rolldownPlugins.
  • LightningCSS. Lightning CSS now autoprefixes and minifies your CSS, in place of Autoprefixer and Stencil's own minifier.
  • OXC. JavaScript is minified with OXC by default. Set jsMinifier: 'terser' to keep using Terser.
  • Your TypeScript. Stencil uses the TypeScript in your project (5.x or 6.x), and no longer ships its own copy.
  • ESM. Stencil's own packages are pure ESM, and the loader-bundle and ssr outputs no longer generate CommonJS by default.
  • Renamed output targets. dist is now loader-bundle, dist-custom-elements is standalone, and dist-hydrate-script is ssr.

Upgrading

Upgrade from the latest Stencil v4:

npm install @stencil/core@rc --save-dev
npx stencil migrate

stencil migrate --dry-run shows what it will change first. Most of the config and decorator changes are automatic, but a few things to look out for:

  • Node.js 22 or later is required.
  • Browser support is now ES2022: Chrome and Edge 94+, Firefox 93+ and Safari 16.4+.
  • Boolean props follow the HTML spec. <my-cmp disabled="false"> now means disabled === true - remove the attribute instead.
  • TypeScript 6 (installed if your project doesn't pin 5.x) rejects "moduleResolution": "node" and turns strict on.
  • ESM only. require('@stencil/core/...') no longer works.

The upgrade guide goes through each step, and the full list of breaking changes explains the reason for every change.

What's Next

Try out Stencil v5 today - and let us know your thoughts or woes.

If something is broken, or behaves differently from v4 (and isn't described in breaking changes), please open an issue or come find me in Discord.

articles.title: How online 2-player works in a browser fighting game: lockstep netcode on a $5 server
articles.description: Hostile Takedown is a parody fighting game that runs in the browser, and it has a "Play a friend"...
articles.body_html:
Hostile Takedown is a parody fighting game that runs in the browser, and it has a "Play a friend" mode: one player creates a room, shares a 4-digit code, and the two of you fight online. Here's how that works without a big game server.

Lockstep instead of a server simulation

The server never runs the fight. Both browsers run the exact same simulation at a fixed 60 steps per second, and the only thing that crosses the network is each player's controller input for each frame, packed into a small bitmask (left, right, duck, block, punch, kick, grab, signature, two supers, jump).

For that to work, both sides must compute identical results from identical inputs. The tricky part is randomness: crits, AI flourishes and particle choices all used Math.random(). During an online match the game swaps it for a small seeded generator (mulberry32), with the seed dealt by the server when the match starts. Purely cosmetic systems (audio, the 3D crowd) keep their own generator so they can't consume numbers from the shared sequence and push the two sides apart.

Hiding latency with input delay

Each input is scheduled a few frames into the future, so it normally reaches the other player before that frame is simulated. The delay isn't fixed: while you wait in the lobby, the host pings the friend through the relay, takes the slower round trips (80th percentile), and sets the delay to cover half of that plus a safety margin, between 4 and 16 frames. Players on the same city network get a snappy game; players across continents get a slightly heavier one that doesn't stall.

Keeping both sides honest

Every 30 frames the host sends a compact snapshot (positions, health, meter, round wins). If the guest has drifted, it nudges its state toward the host's using its own history for that frame. Rendering is interpolated between simulation steps, so motion stays smooth on 120 Hz phones and when a frame occasionally has to wait for a late input.

Phones and dropped connections

Phones kill WebSockets the moment you switch apps to send the room code. Each seat gets a secret token stored in the browser, and the server holds a dropped seat for 90 seconds, so you can share the link on WhatsApp, come back and still be the host. If a connection drops in the middle of a fight, both players return to the pick screen with the same CEOs instead of the match silently desyncing.

The server

The relay is about 200 lines of dependency-free Node: a minimal WebSocket implementation on Node's own http module, rooms with two seats, a heartbeat, and message relaying. It runs on a $5/month Lightsail instance behind Caddy for HTTPS.

If you try the online mode with a friend, I'd love to hear how it felt on your connection: play Hostile Takedown.

articles.title: My music API refused 145 songs for naming an artist. A third of those artists were ordinary words
articles.description: An AI song generator in 24 languages, 2.5 years of moderation refusals, and what an artist-name filter does to words like rhythm, wind, heavy and cat. Plus the small fixes: a replacement list, an automatic retry, and a message the user can act on.
articles.body_html:
I run a small AI song generator. People describe a song, or paste their own lyrics plus a style line ("acoustic guitar, warm female vocals"), and a third-party music generation API turns that into a track. Most of my users don't write in English: the biggest groups are Ukrainian, Slovak, Polish and Czech, and the site runs in 24 languages.

The API has one rule that shows up in my error logs again and again: no artist names. You can ask for "80s synth pop", not for a song "like" a named band. Fair enough. The trouble is what the filter thinks an artist name is.

Last week a quality check flagged six paid generations in four days that had failed with an artist-name refusal. Five of them were the same word: rytmus. In Slovak and Czech that just means rhythm. One user wrote "acoustic guitar, rytmus", got refused three times in a row, then changed it to "rhythm" and got the song. Another wrote "a slower rhythm, strong bass, r&b" in Slovak, was refused twice, and never generated again.

So I went back through every refusal in the database.

The numbers

From May 2024 to mid-November 2026 the site sent about 4,500 generations. 145 came back refused for an artist name.

Period Generations Refused for artist name
May–Sep 2024 3,644 138 (3.8 %)
Oct 2024–Nov 2025 259 0
Dec 2025–Nov 2026 637 7 (1.1 %)

The quiet middle period had little traffic, so I won't read much into the zero. The 2024 refusals were mostly on the free-text song description (112), the rest on the style tags (26). All 7 recent ones were on the style tags.

Then I read the 145 names the filter reported, and sorted them by hand.

  • Real artists, asked for on purpose: the majority. Pop stars, classic rock bands, rappers, a few metal bands. The filter was right, and the user needed a better hint (more on that below).
  • Ordinary words: 49 of 145, by my reading. About a third.
  • First names of the person the song was for: at least 4. On a site where people make birthday and anniversary songs, that one hurts.

The ordinary words

These are words that the filter reported as an artist name, with what they mean in the language the user wrote in:

Reported "artist" Language Meaning Times
melodico Italian melodic 9
latino Spanish Latin (as in Latin pop) 6
rytmus Slovak / Czech rhythm 5
pesado Portuguese heavy 3
wiatr Polish wind 2
epica Portuguese (épica) epic 2
sin miedo Spanish without fear 2
bebe Portuguese (bebê) baby 2
salvador Portuguese saviour (in a hymn) 2
gato Portuguese cat 1
letto Italian bed 1
catedral Portuguese cathedral 1
havasi Turkish (havası) tune, air 1
devochka Russian (девочка) little girl 1
nhac thieu nhi Vietnamese (nhạc thiếu nhi) children's music 1
tage German days 1
trunks English an elephant's trunks, in a zoo song 1

Plus a handful of single cases like roadtrip, menor (minor), rico (rich), libera (sets free), vedo (I see), levante (rise).

Most of these are genre and mood words, which is exactly what the API asks you to write instead of artist names. "Pop rock melodico italiano" is a textbook style description. It was refused nine times.

The filter folds the text before it matches

Look at the right-hand spelling in the table. The user wrote épica, bebê, Havası, девочка, Nhạc thiếu nhi. The refusal reported epica, bebe, havasi, devochka, nhac thieu nhi.

So the filter strips accents (Vietnamese tone marks included) and transliterates Cyrillic into plain Latin letters, and only then compares against its list of names. That is why it catches so much outside English: once every word is folded to ASCII, a lot of common words in other languages land on a band or a stage name somewhere. A Russian rap prompt that mentioned a well-known American rapper in the genitive case came back as rossa: folded and transliterated, inflection included.

Two practical consequences for anyone sending user text to a filtered API:

  1. If you keep a list of known false positives, match it on folded text too, or you'll miss the accented forms users really type.
  2. Your users can't predict this. "Write genres and moods, not artist names" is good advice that still fails for an Italian writing melodico.

What I changed

Three small things, in order of how often they help.

1. Replace known false positives before submitting. A short, explicit list, only words that have actually been refused. It is applied to the style line in the generate route:

const FALSE_ARTIST_WORDS: Record<string, string> = {
  rytmus: "rhythm", // sk/cs; 5 refusals in Nov 2026
};

const escapeRe = (s: string) => s.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, "\\$&");
// \b doesn't know č or š, so use Unicode letter boundaries
const wordRe = (word: string) =>
  new RegExp(`(?<![\\p{L}\\p{N}])${escapeRe(word)}(?![\\p{L}\\p{N}])`, "giu");

export function replaceFalseArtistWords(style: string): string {
  let out = style;
  for (const [word, repl] of Object.entries(FALSE_ARTIST_WORDS)) {
    out = out.replace(wordRe(word), repl);
  }
  return out;
}

The \b detail matters. In JavaScript, \b only understands ASCII word characters, so it sees a word boundary between č and the next letter, and \brytmus\b can match the tail of a longer word. The lookarounds with \p{L} (any letter, needs the u flag) fix that.

The list starts with one word on purpose. Replacing a word changes what the user asked for, so each entry has to be a confirmed refusal with an obvious English equivalent. melodico → melodic and pesado → heavy are the next candidates from the table above.

2. Retry once without the name. The refusal arrives in the provider's async callback. The generate route now keeps the submitted parameters on the job row, so the callback can strip the reported word from the style line and resubmit:

const artist = artistFromRefusal(refusal.msg);   // "rytmus", "bon jovi", ...
const style = stripArtist(req.style, artist);    // also tidies leftover commas and slashes
if (!style || style === req.style || retries.length >= 2) return false; // fall back to fail + refund
// resubmit with the same params and the new style; the song stays "processing"

Rules I set: only for the style field in custom mode, at most two retries per song (one prompt named two bands), never when stripping leaves the style empty, and the user is not charged again. If the retry can't run, the old path applies: the song fails and the credit goes back.

I deliberately do not retry refusals on the free-text description. Removing a word from "a song for my wife ___ for our anniversary" can remove the one word the song is about.

An honest gap: going through the old rows for this post showed the provider has changed the wording of this error at least twice. In 2024 it was moderation_failure; Tags contained artist name: X or Song Description contained artist name: X. Since December 2025 it is Your tags contain artist name X - we don't reference specific artists. My parser only knows the current one. If the wording changes again, the retry silently stops working and everything falls back to fail-and-refund. Accepting all three formats, plus an alert when a refusal arrives that the parser can't read, is the next change. The retry has also not fired in production yet, so I can't report its success rate.

3. Tell the user what happened, in their language. Before, a refused song just showed up as failed, at best with the provider's raw English message. Now the owner sees, on the song page and in their song list, a sentence like:

The music AI doesn't accept artist names in "Music Style Tag" ("rytmus"). Describe the sound with genres and moods instead, e.g. "pop rock, warm male vocals".

It uses the same label as the form field in each of the 24 languages, so people know which box to edit. For the real artist requests, which are the majority, this is the fix that matters. Most of those users weren't trying to copy anyone; they used a famous name as shorthand for a sound, because that's how people describe music to each other.

What I'd tell someone building on a filtered generation API

  • Log the refusal reason with the request. I could only do this analysis because the full response was stored next to each job. Without it, 145 refusals would have been 145 anonymous failures.
  • Group refusals by language. Moderation tuned on English text behaves differently once it folds everything to ASCII. Look at the words, not just the count.
  • Parse provider error messages defensively. Match more than one wording, and alert when nothing matches, because a silent parser failure looks exactly like "no refusals".
  • Treat the error text as product copy. The person who hit the filter needs to know which field to change and what to write instead.

The site, if you want to see the form these style lines go into: AISong.Fun.
